clinicalPearls: The commonest form of intestinal ischaemia, usually a transient, non-occlusive reduction in colonic perfusion
Presents with sudden crampy abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhoea, typically in older patients
Watershed areas such as the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction are most vulnerable
It is usually self-limiting, unlike acute mesenteric ischaemia of the small bowel, which is a surgical emergency
CT may show colonic wall thickening, and colonoscopy shows segmental mucosal changes
Most cases resolve with supportive care, but gangrenous or fulminant colitis needs surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Ischaemic colitis results from a temporary compromise of colonic blood flow that is insufficient to meet metabolic demand, most often non-occlusive and related to a low-flow state, with the poorly collateralised watershed regions most affected. Mucosal injury ranges from reversible superficial changes to transmural infarction. Precipitants include hypotension, hypovolaemia, cardiac failure, vasoconstrictors and, in younger patients, causes such as vasculitis, thrombophilia, cocaine use and strenuous exertion.
additionalInvestigations: CT of the abdomen with contrast
Colonoscopy showing segmental changes (avoided if peritonitis)
Blood tests including lactate and inflammatory markers
Assessment for a precipitating low-flow or thrombotic cause
redFlags: Peritonitis or signs of transmural infarction
Rising lactate, acidosis or systemic toxicity
Right-sided (isolated) ischaemic colitis, which behaves more aggressively
Failure to improve, suggesting gangrene or stricture
reference.prognosis: Most transient cases resolve within days with supportive care; gangrenous or fulminant colitis carries significant mortality, and some develop a chronic segment or stricture.
pitfalls: Confusing it with acute mesenteric ischaemia and delaying surgery when the small bowel is involved
Mistaking it for infective colitis or inflammatory bowel disease
Performing colonoscopy in a patient with peritonitis
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
